extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of medieval history / Crusades source criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for classifying, assessing, and prioritizing primary and secondary sources for the Crusades (eye‑witness accounts, later compilations, legendary narratives, chronicles, legal documents, and modern bibliographies). Emphasizes authorial standpoint, contemporaneity, genre, bias, and textual transmission issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounts of eye-witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary, first-hand narratives written by participants (the anonymous author of the Gesta Francorum, Raymund of Agiles, Fulcher of Chartres, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued as primary authorities because they are eye-witness throughout and contemporary—often written practically at the time of events. Consider author's social/status perspective (layman vs clerk), geographic/political point of view (Norman, Provencal, Lotharingian), presence/absence at particular events (affects reliability for specific episodes), and the complementary value of different eyewitnesses. Example guidance: the Anonymus Gesta is 'primary authority' and represents the ordinary crusader; Raymund gives an ecclesiastic/Provencal view; Fulcher complements the others though he may be absent for parts of the First Crusade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later compilations based on primary accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Redactions and artistic reworkings that build on earlier accounts (e.g., redactors of the Gesta such as Guibert of Nogent, Balderich of Dol, Robert of Reims; Tudebod accused of plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These works often try to 'mend' uncouth style and may confess indebtedness or plagiarize. They can be more polished and popular in the Middle Ages but are derivative—useful for transmission and reception history, less authoritative for original facts. Beware of asserted priority (e.g., claims that Tudebod was the original) and distinguish honest redaction from plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi‑legendary and legendary narratives (saga)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives arising from storytelling, idolization, and religious impulse that heighten, mythologize, or introduce miraculous elements (e.g., Albert of Aix, Chanson des chetifs, Chanson d'Antioche)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legend grows quickly—features include inconsistencies, chronological/topographical errors, poetical colour and vivid battle-scene description. Legends can pervert truth (e.g., misdating of events, exaggerated roles). Use legends cautiously: valuable for cultural/mentalité and reception, but not as straightforward factual authorities. Recognize causes: storytelling instinct, idolization, religious interpretation of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: William of Tyre as a scientific historian
rubrics_metrics.description: William of Tyre is characterised as 'rather a scientific historian than a chronicler' who weaves eyewitness accounts and saga details into a harmonious narrative (Historia rerum in partibus transmarinis gestarum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He is eclectic—choosing material to 'weave a pleasant narrative' rather than applying strict critical principles. His work is a real authority mainly from the Second Crusade onward. Strengths: educated, had archives, diligent, impartial, well-informed, stylistically excellent. Weaknesses: reception of legendary elements, occasional bias toward picturesque material, and vagueness in chronology. Use him as authoritative for later periods and for narrative synthesis, but check his sources and chronological precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eastern (Byzantine, Arabic, Armenian) authorities and how to weight them
rubrics_metrics.description: Non‑Western sources (e.g., Anna Comnena's Alexiad, Matthew of Edessa, Arabic chronicles like Ibn Athir, Kemal‑ud‑din's History of Aleppo, Vie d'Ousama) provide corrective or complementary perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alexiad is especially important as a corrective to Western prejudice (and brings Bohemund into prominence). Armenian chronicles present local/national perspectives (e.g., Matthew of Edessa on Edessa). Arabic writings tend to be later, religious in purpose, and stylistically colder, but are often written by men of affairs (governors, secretaries, ambassadors) and can record events impartially (fatalistic temper). Value depends on date, authorial position, and intended audience—use them for balance and to understand Muslim/Byzantine viewpoints, especially from the 12th century onward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish official/apologetic narratives from non‑official soldier accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate accounts written by leaders or defenders of controversial actions (e.g., Villehardouin's La Conquete de Constantinople—an official apology) from ordinary soldier/participant narratives (e.g., Robert de Clari's La Prise de Constantinople).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess authorial role and motive: apologetic/official accounts may conceal 'arcana' or present self-justifying narratives; non-official soldier accounts may offer more candid or divergent perspectives. Use both to triangulate events and to understand intended audience and rhetorical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary authorities by crusade (recommended principal sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each major crusade the article lists principal contemporary sources considered primary (e.g., First Crusade: Gesta Francorum, Raymund, Fulcher; Second: Odo de Deuil, Otto of Freising, letters of Louis VII; Third: Ambroise's Carmen, Itinerarium Peregrinorum, French and German chroniclers; Fourth: Villehardouin, Robert de Clari; later crusades: continuations of William of Tyre, Jacques de Vitry, Marino Sanudo, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When researching a particular crusade, consult the listed primary authorities for that campaign and note their national/clerical/professional viewpoints. Use the combination of national traditions (Anglo‑Norman, French, German, Byzantine, Arabic, Armenian) to build a multi‑vocal account. Be mindful of plagiarism/transmission relations among texts (e.g., Itinerarium is largely a translation of Ambroise's Carmen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Documents and administrative records (charters, cartularies, coins, seals, monuments, genealogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material documents bearing on Crusader history include charters (Regesta regni Hierosolymitani, cartularies of the Hospitaliers and Church of the Holy Sepulchre), coins and seals, monuments of military architecture, and genealogical books (Livre des lignages d'outre‑mer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These documentary materials are crucial for institutional, constitutional, social and material history (e.g., genealogy of the Levant, coins/seals for economic history, monuments for architecture). Use published editions (Rohricht, Delaville‑Leroulx, de Roziere, Schlumberger, Rey) and evaluate authenticity, provenance, and editorial apparatus. Combine documentary evidence with narrative sources for fuller picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assizes, law‑books and legal sources: treat as custumals/law‑books not original codes
rubrics_metrics.description: The assizes of the kingdom (high court and court of burgesses) survive largely as law‑books written by legists (John of Ibelin, Philip of Novara, Geoffrey of Tort) rather than as contemporaneous codified laws; they involve later recensions and glosses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these texts as lawyers' reconstructions or expositions (custumals), often written after the loss of the kingdom, not straightforward original statutes. Be cautious of claims (the 'Letters of the Sepulchre', Godfrey as nomothetes) which may be myth-making. Textual transmission issues: recensions and revisions (noted reworkings in 1368 and 1531), glosses, and use in Cyprus mean the surviving text may be late and layered—critically assess textual history and editorial interventions before using as evidence of original legal practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modern bibliographies and secondary scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern works and bibliographies (e.g., A. Molinier Les Sources de l'histoire de France, von Sybel, Hagenmeyer's editions, Rohricht, Kugler, Brehier, Stevenson's The Crusaders in the East, Dodu, Rey, Prutz) are essential guides to the original authorities and to interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with comprehensive bibliographies and modern critical editions of primary sources. Consult scholarly prefaces and editions (Hagenmeyer for the Gesta and Ekkehard) for source criticism, and modern syntheses (Rohricht, von Sybel, Brehier) for historiographical orientation. Use recommended secondary works for chronology issues, constitutional and social history, and Eastern affairs; always check them against primary source editions.
